extracted.intended_audience: general readers and journalists (news consumers, editors, reporters)
extracted.subtask_short: reporting and broadcast standards for news
extracted.subtask_description: An AP newswire collection of international and domestic items that includes statements of broadcasting policy, standards for presenting atrocity evidence, and procedural conditions for government actions; useful for extracting journalistic and broadcast guidance embedded in reporting. Mostly aimed at informing the public and communicating official positions/policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice of America credibility and factuality
rubrics_metrics.description: "People who risk their lives to listen are entitled to the truth"; the Voice will emphasize factual news reporting instead of "violently anti-Soviet criticism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USIA chief stated VOA broadcasts to the Soviet Union should gain "creditability" and a reputation for factual reporting; avoid violent ideological attacks. This is presented as a principal policy for producing trustworthy international broadcasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiated messaging for satellite nations
rubrics_metrics.description: A different approach will be made to the people of satellite nations: these listeners "will be encouraged in their 'hope for liberation.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USIA policy distinguishes target audiences and tailors content: while Soviet-wide broadcasts emphasize factuality, broadcasts to satellite nations may include content fostering aspiration or dissent (encouraging 'hope for liberation').

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast content standard — no obscene language on air
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio stations are accountable when an obscene word is heard on the air; employees may be suspended. (Example: two employees of radio station WWDC were suspended because of an obscene word that got out of the broadcast.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stations must prevent obscene material from being broadcast (technical controls, prompt cut-offs). If an incident occurs, networks typically assume responsibility, issue apologies, and may suspend staff and engineers involved; prompt remedial statements to listeners are expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Station accountability and remediation for on-air incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Network spokesmen assumed "full responsibility" for an accidental obscene on-air remark and issued apologies to listeners; stations are expected to investigate, identify technical failures, and apologize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting responsibility, investigating the technical cause (e.g., failure to cut off a live microphone), offering public apology, and disciplining or suspending staff are presented as proper remediation steps following broadcast failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard for atrocity reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The Army's report of atrocities was "documented with photographs and eye-witness stories."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting grave charges (e.g., war crimes, atrocities) to international bodies or the public, documentation with photographic evidence and eyewitness accounts is portrayed as essential to establish credibility and support calls for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for resumption of foreign aid (procedural requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. aid to Israel was reported to be resumed "as a result of the latter's agreement to halt work on [the Jordan hydroelectric] project."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resumption of bilateral assistance may be conditioned on host-country actions or concessions; public statements link aid decisions to specific policy changes (here, stopping a disputed project) and such conditions are presented as explicit prerequisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burmese government standard for evacuation acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Burmese government said it will not consider anything short of "total evacuation as satisfactory" regarding withdrawal of designated groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When governments articulate terms for acceptable outcomes in negotiations or withdrawals, they may set absolute standards (e.g., total evacuation) which function as non-negotiable criteria for acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.N. procedural requirement when placing issues on the Assembly agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. experts went into a huddle to write a "required explanatory memorandum" telling why the United States considered it vital to put the army report on the Assembly agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting matters for U.N. consideration often requires accompanying explanatory documentation that justifies agenda placement; preparing such memoranda is treated as a necessary procedural step.
